paragraphs.heading: Checking the theory
paragraphs.text: Tests of general relativity are the observations that give the theory its evidence. Einstein proposed the first three in 1915: the unexplained shift in Mercury's orbit, the bending of light by gravity, and the gravitational redshift. Mercury's shift was already known. Light bending was measured in 1919 and ever more precisely after that, and although redshift was claimed in 1925, measurements sensitive enough to confirm it came only in 1954.

paragraphs.heading: Mercury's wandering orbit
paragraphs.text: In Newton's physics, a body orbiting a round mass traces an ellipse, and its point of closest approach, called the periapsis, or perihelion when the central body is the Sun, stays fixed. In the real Solar System, planets' perihelia rotate around the Sun. The main cause is the planets tugging on each other's orbits, with a much smaller part played by solar oblateness. Mercury's perihelion moves differently from what these Newtonian effects predict.

paragraphs.heading: The planet that wasn't
paragraphs.text: Urbain Le Verrier flagged the problem in 1859, finding a mismatch of 38 arcseconds per century, later revised to 43 by Simon Newcomb. He suggested an unseen planet might explain it, and since Neptune had been found from its pull on Uranus, astronomers placed some faith in the idea, and the planet was even given a name, Vulcan. No evidence of Vulcan was ever found. Einstein's 1915 theory explained the extra shift as gravity acting through curved spacetime, and it agreed closely with the observed amount.

paragraphs.heading: Starlight bent by the Sun
paragraphs.text: Henry Cavendish in 1784 and Johann Georg von Soldner in 1801 noted that Newton's gravity predicts starlight bending around a massive object. Einstein got Soldner's value in 1911 using the equivalence principle alone. In 1915, while completing general relativity, he saw that this was only half the correct value. The 1919 measurements of light bending matched the new prediction.

paragraphs.heading: Stronger fields
paragraphs.text: Starting in 1959, a more accurate program tested the theory where gravity is weak and severely limited any departures from it. In the 1970s Irwin Shapiro measured the extra delay of radar signals passing near the Sun. From 1974 Russell Hulse, Joseph Taylor and others studied binary pulsars, whose gravity is much stronger than anything in the Solar System. In weak fields and strong ones alike, the theory's predictions have been extremely well tested.

paragraphs.heading: Other planets and pulsars
paragraphs.text: Other planets' perihelia shift too, but by less, because they are farther from the Sun and take longer to orbit. Earth's shift due to general relativity is predicted at 3.83868 arcseconds per century and measured at 3.8387 ± 0.0004. In the binary pulsar PSR 1913+16 the same kind of shift reaches 4.2° per year, and that too fits general relativity.

paragraphs.heading: Waves from black holes
paragraphs.text: In February 2016 the Advanced LIGO team announced that it had directly detected gravitational waves from two black holes merging. Along with further detections announced in 2016 and 2017, this tested the theory where gravity is very strong, and so far no deviations have been seen. The theory sets itself a high bar. Its appeal lies in its logical completeness, and if even one of its conclusions proved wrong, it would have to be given up, since changing it without wrecking the whole structure seems to be impossible.
